rationale: Start with a broad mid-length scouting gradient at moderate temperature to capture all 10 compounds and map the elution window while reducing risk of a truncated run. This should show whether peaks are compressed early, late, or across the full range so later injections can tighten the window and adjust slope.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only way to improve CRF is to shorten the run while keeping the weakest pair above 1.5. A modest step to a steeper gradient should pull the last peak earlier and test how much resolution margin the critical mid-cluster can spare.

The current method is very close to ideal, with the last peak only slightly past 10 min and the worst pair still above 1.5. A small further reduction in tG is the most direct way to try to eliminate the time penalty while checking whether the critical 6/7 pair remains acceptable.

The critical pair appears nearly slope-limited, so keep the fast 14 min gradient and use a small temperature drop to try to improve selectivity for the 6/7 pair while staying under 10 min for the last peak. This directly tests whether temperature can recover full resolution without reintroducing a time penalty.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity badly, so probe the opposite direction while keeping the fast 14 min gradient that gave a zero time penalty. If 45 C improves the crowded mid-cluster, it could restore full pair credit without pushing the last peak past 10 min.

The peaks elute within a narrow solvent-strength band, so trimming the gradient window should make the gradient shallower in the region that matters and may recover the critical mid-cluster resolution without lengthening the run much. This tests whether window compression is better than changing temperature for the near-coeluting pair(s).

Now that full score has been reached, the useful next move is to map the edge by shortening tG one step while keeping the successful window and temperature. This checks whether the method can be made faster while preserving all pairs at or above 1.5, or identifies the immediate back-off point.

tG 12 was too steep, so keep the successful 14 min slope basis and tighten the upper end slightly to see if the last peak can be pulled just under 10.00 min while preserving the critical 6/7 resolution. The last peak was eluting essentially at the gradient end, so a small phi1 reduction may improve score margin without strongly disturbing the mid-cluster.

Raising phi0 should shorten the run by reducing early low-retention time while keeping the shallower, successful mid-cluster slope from the 0.10–0.85 window. This tests whether the first peaks have excess margin that can be traded for a small improvement in the last-peak time without sacrificing the critical 6/7 pair.

Injection 9 gives full score with only a small resolution margin at the critical pair, so the next step is to locate the faster boundary from this improved window. Shortening tG by one step tests whether the 6/7 pair stays at or above 1.5 while gaining additional runtime efficiency.

The 0.15–0.85, 14 min method is already optimal by CRF, so this run probes nearby robustness by slightly widening the upper end while keeping the same slope region and temperature. It tests whether the critical pair gains margin or the late peak shifts unfavorably, helping confirm whether injection 9 is the best operating point.

The best region appears near injection 9, so raise phi0 one more step while holding phi1 and tG to see if early dead time can be reduced further without hurting the critical 6/7 selectivity. This is a targeted test of whether the lower end of the gradient window can be trimmed more aggressively while retaining full pair credit.

Injection 9 is excellent, so now test whether trimming the upper end by one step from that optimum can preserve the critical mid-cluster resolution while maybe still staying within full-score territory. This helps bracket the best window around the current optimum without changing temperature or gradient time.

Injection 9 already achieves the maximum CRF, so use remaining budget to probe robustness around that optimum. A small temperature increase may further shorten the run, and even if CRF cannot exceed 1.000 it helps determine whether the best method is stable or highly temperature-sensitive near the critical 6/7 pair.

A longer gradient at the current best window should increase margin on the critical 6/7 pair and confirm the slope dependence around the optimum, even though it will likely incur a small time penalty. This helps map robustness and gives a safer alternative if resolution reserve is preferred over minimum runtime.

The remaining untested local variant around the best window is a lower temperature, which may shift selectivity differently than the higher-temperature failure and define robustness around the optimum. This checks whether 40 C is uniquely favorable for the 6/7 pair or whether there is a cooler full-score alternative.

The data show 40 C is the sweet spot and the best methods lie near a 14 min gradient with a moderately trimmed window; this final nearby window test checks whether balancing both ends at 0.10–0.90 offers a broader robustness margin while still potentially maintaining full score. It helps confirm whether 0.15–0.85 is truly the best-centered operating point.

One remaining informative local check is to keep the successful higher phi0 from injection 9 while expanding only the upper end to the original broad finish. This will show whether late-strength excess improves or worsens the critical 6/7 selectivity relative to the two full-score methods and further confirm the optimum window placement.

This is a robustness check around the other full-score method, increasing tG one step to see how much extra margin the 6/7 pair gains when the slope is relaxed at the 0.10–0.85 window. It helps compare the two CRF-optimal windows on resolution reserve versus runtime sensitivity.

A lower phi0 than the full-score methods has not been tested with the successful trimmed upper end, so this run checks whether extra early retention can improve the critical cluster enough to offset any last-peak delay. It completes the local window map around the best 14 min, 40 C condition.

This completes the immediate neighborhood around the best method by combining the higher phi0 and higher phi1 changes that individually reduced the critical-pair margin. It will confirm whether their effects are roughly additive and further validate injection 9 as the most balanced window.

Among the narrower-window variants, 0.10–0.80 had excellent resolution but a slight time penalty; lengthening tG here will show whether that extra margin grows as expected and whether this window is fundamentally too retentive for top CRF. It rounds out the slope map for a potentially robust alternative window.

With only a few runs left, this fills in the last obvious untested broad-upper-window combination near the explored optimum region. It will confirm how much the balance of lower and upper window limits contributes to the critical 6/7 margin compared with the two full-score methods.

One remaining useful edge test is a further increase in phi0 from the best 0.15–0.85 method, which should compress the early part more and reveal whether the optimum is limited by the first compounds becoming too unretained or by loss of the critical 6/7 selectivity. It tightens the lower-bound map around the best window.

For the final shot, test a still narrower upper window from the best method to see whether the extra shallowing can preserve or improve the critical 6/7 margin while keeping the last peak under 10 min. It is the last untested adjacent window around the proven optimum at 0.15–0.85, 14 min, 40 C.
